findings.title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches SpawnProcess, so hung flushers are never killed
findings.body: Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new guard means a hung process (cause="hang") is never killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement. The old process keeps running against the same Redis shards alongside the new one, and the `ValueError` handling no longer matters. The same broken check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')` / `isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` negated, or check against `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`.

findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: The test starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", does nothing. The flusher thread has no guaranteed time to flush before `step.join()` sets `stopped`. `assert (msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently. Wait with a real sleep (capture the original `time.sleep` before patching), or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

findings.title: join() stops terminating remaining processes once the deadline is hit
findings.body: When the deadline expires the loop `break`s. The remaining processes are neither waited on nor terminated, because `terminate()` sits inside the loop body after the wait. With several processes, the later ones are left running (or killed only by daemon semantics). Terminate all processes after the wait phase regardless of the deadline.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag name `shards` vs `shard`
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use the tag `shard`, while `wait_produce` uses `shards`. `flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard` with a single int. The value is a comma-joined list of shards when a process owns several. This makes dashboards and aggregations inconsistent and produces high-cardinality tag values. Use one tag name and consistent semantics.

findings.title: Unused `_create_process_for_shard` method
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called. Remove the dead code.
